briefs.area: Reconciling partial putaway against a single receipt balance
briefs.readerQuestion: How should a putaway task be recorded when only part of a received quantity has been moved to storage?
evidence: A putaway record should distinguish the quantity already placed in storage from the balance still awaiting a destination, rather than closing the receipt when the first movement is recorded.
The receiving record and the putaway task should remain linked so the same physical units are not counted as both received and still outstanding.
A parent receipt should not be marked complete while a child putaway task still shows an unplaced balance.

reviewedPlan.title: Recording Partial Putaway Without Closing the Receipt
reviewedPlan.description: How to keep a receipt open while only part of the received quantity has been moved into storage.
reviewedPlan.excerpt: A partial putaway should show placed and unplaced quantities separately, stay linked to the receipt, and not close the parent record early.
reviewedPlan.keyAnswer: A putaway task that has moved only part of a received quantity should record the placed quantity and the balance still awaiting a destination. The receipt should stay open and linked to that task so the same units are not counted twice. The parent receipt should not be closed while an unplaced balance remains.
operationalBasis: A putaway record should distinguish the quantity already placed in storage from the balance still awaiting a destination, rather than closing the receipt when the first movement is recorded.
The receiving record and the putaway task should remain linked so the same physical units are not counted as both received and still outstanding.
A parent receipt should not be marked complete while a child putaway task still shows an unplaced balance.
reviewedPlan.searchIntent: How should a putaway task be recorded when only part of a received quantity has been moved to storage?
outline: Separating placed quantity from the unplaced balance
Keeping the putaway task linked to its receipt
Why the parent receipt stays open
Confirming the destination balance before closing

review.rationale: Every evidence statement is a reasonable conditional deduction from the cited foundations: partial-completion supports separating placed quantity from the unplaced balance and not closing a parent record while a child task is incomplete; physical-record-alignment supports keeping the receipt and putaway task linked so the same physical units are not counted twice. The decision is distinct from published and unused briefs, which cover partial shipment permissions, unloading-sequence receipt balances, receipt-reference splits and carton-content amendments, but none address recording a partially completed putaway against a single receipt balance while keeping the parent receipt open.

briefs.area: Handling a retry of a warehouse task message already accepted
briefs.readerQuestion: How should a retried warehouse task message be checked so it does not create a second physical task for work already accepted?
evidence: A retry should preserve the identity of the original business request so the receiver can recognise work already accepted rather than treating the message as new.
Work already accepted should be distinguished from work still pending, so a retry does not silently generate another physical task.
A successful transmission should be distinguished from accepted business processing before the retry is treated as complete.

reviewedPlan.title: Checking a Retried Task Message Before It Repeats Work
reviewedPlan.description: How to confirm a retried warehouse task message does not create a duplicate physical task.
reviewedPlan.excerpt: A retry should keep the original request identity, separate accepted from pending work, and not treat transmission as acceptance.
reviewedPlan.keyAnswer: A retried task message should carry the identity of the original business request so already accepted work is recognised. Accepted work should be separated from work still pending before the retry is processed. Successful transmission alone should not be treated as accepted business processing.
operationalBasis: A retry should preserve the identity of the original business request so the receiver can recognise work already accepted rather than treating the message as new.
Work already accepted should be distinguished from work still pending, so a retry does not silently generate another physical task.
A successful transmission should be distinguished from accepted business processing before the retry is treated as complete.
reviewedPlan.searchIntent: How should a retried warehouse task message be checked so it does not create a second physical task for work already accepted?
outline: Separating accepted work from pending work
Recording the retry outcome against the original request

review.rationale: Every evidence statement is a reasonable conditional deduction from the cited foundations: retry-continuity directly supports preserving the original business request identity, distinguishing accepted from pending work, and not creating a second physical task; interface-contracts supports distinguishing successful transmission from accepted business processing. The decision is distinct from published and unused briefs such as order-import-deduplication, partial-file-import-results, incremental-export-watermarks and failed-message-quarantine, which cover resubmitted order files, partial row acceptance, export boundaries and quarantined messages, but not checking a retried warehouse task message against already accepted work to avoid a duplicate physical task.

briefs.area: Interpreting an availability statement that mixes confirmed and unconfirmed stock
briefs.readerQuestion: How should an availability statement be read when some quantities are confirmed and others are not?
evidence: An availability statement should separate known, unconfirmed, committed and physically observed quantities.
Missing confirmation should not be converted into an assumed positive availability.
A commitment should be based on the quantity basis and observation boundary stated, not on a total that mixes categories.

reviewedPlan.title: Reading Availability When Confirmed and Unconfirmed Quantities Are Mixed
reviewedPlan.description: A conditional method for separating confirmed, unconfirmed and committed quantities before acting on an availability statement.
reviewedPlan.excerpt: Split known, unconfirmed, committed and observed quantities, avoid treating missing confirmation as available, and state the observation boundary.
reviewedPlan.keyAnswer: An availability statement should separate known, unconfirmed, committed and physically observed quantities rather than presenting one total. Missing confirmation should not be read as available stock, and any commitment should rest on the stated quantity basis and observation boundary.
operationalBasis: An availability statement should separate known, unconfirmed, committed and physically observed quantities.
Missing confirmation should not be converted into an assumed positive availability.
A commitment should be based on the quantity basis and observation boundary stated, not on a total that mixes categories.
reviewedPlan.searchIntent: How should an availability statement be read when some quantities are confirmed and others are not?
outline: Why missing confirmation is not availability
Basing commitments on the right category

review.rationale: Each evidence statement is a reasonable conditional deduction from availability-qualifications, quantity-basis and reporting-boundaries. The decision—how to read an availability statement that mixes confirmed, unconfirmed, committed and physically observed quantities, and refuse to treat missing confirmation as available—is a distinct operational decision not covered by the published stock-reservation, blank-zero-field or reporting briefs.

briefs.area: Keeping client ownership distinct when a shared work assignment changes
briefs.readerQuestion: When a shared warehouse work assignment changes, what should show that stock ownership has not moved?
evidence: Client ownership and access should remain distinguishable from physical product identity and location.
Changing a contact or shared work assignment should not itself transfer stock ownership.
Where ownership is unclear, the question should be resolved before stock is treated as another client's.

reviewedPlan.title: Keeping Stock Ownership Clear When Work Assignments Change
reviewedPlan.description: A conditional check that separates a change in work assignment or contact from any change in stock ownership.
reviewedPlan.excerpt: Treat assignment and contact changes as operational, keep ownership tied to its original reference, and resolve unclear ownership before reassigning stock.
reviewedPlan.keyAnswer: A change in a shared work assignment or client contact should not by itself move stock ownership. Ownership should stay tied to its original business reference, and unclear ownership should be resolved before stock is treated as belonging to another client.
operationalBasis: Client ownership and access should remain distinguishable from physical product identity and location.
Changing a contact or shared work assignment should not itself transfer stock ownership.
Where ownership is unclear, the question should be resolved before stock is treated as another client's.
reviewedPlan.searchIntent: When a shared warehouse work assignment changes, what should show that stock ownership has not moved?
outline: What a work assignment change does and does not do

review.rationale: Grounded in client-ownership and entity-identity; the statements follow conditionally from the foundation. The decision—separating a work-assignment or contact change from any transfer of stock ownership, and resolving unclear ownership before reassignment—is distinct from the approved client-access-removal-review and inventory-owner-separation briefs, which address access removal and identical-goods ownership respectively rather than assignment-change ownership confusion.
